title: What is the P/B Ratio?
subtitle: Market value versus book value - when should you use it?
openingOptions: The market is valuing the stock below book value - it may be undervalued or the industry may be struggling
The company is about to go bankrupt
explanation: P/B compares market capitalization against the book value of shareholders' equity - the price the market pays versus what accounting records. Below one means the market is valuing a business below its net assets on the books - sometimes an opportunity, but more often the market is saying those assets earn poorly or aren't worth as much as the books claim. So P/B only means something when read alongside ROE, and only fits industries where book value is close to real value.

diagram.label: < 1: cheaper than net assets - check the reason why

realWorldExample.company: Bank stocks during the 2008-2012 crisis period
realWorldExample.description: During the 2011-2013 Vietnamese bank bad-debt crisis, many bank stocks traded at a P/B below 1 - the market was worried real asset quality (hidden bad debt) was much worse than the numbers on the books, not simply that 'the stock was cheap.'

quiz.question: P/B is best suited for valuing which industry?
options: Retail - because inventory is always recorded at market price
Pharma - because R&D costs are all capitalized into book value
Banks, insurance, real estate - assets make up most of the value
Tech startups - because value sits in already-recorded intellectual property
quiz.explanation: P/B is useful when book-value assets reflect real value accurately (banks: loan portfolios; real estate: land assets). For tech/software, a low book value doesn't reflect brand value and IP.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a bank with P/B = 0.7 automatically represent an attractive value-investing opportunity?
options: A P/B below 1 is always a good opportunity, so you should buy right away when you see this ratio
A P/B below 1 only happens to a bank that's forced into mandatory bankruptcy
No further analysis is needed - if P/B is low, just buy and hold long term
You need to check asset quality - unrecognized bad debt can make the book value illusory
quiz.explanation: A low P/B can be a 'value trap' if the published book value doesn't accurately reflect real asset quality - especially important for banks, where most assets are loans that may hide bad debt not yet fully provisioned for.

quiz.question: Market cap is 1,400 billion, book value of equity is 2,000 billion. What is the P/B?
options: 0.7x (= 1,400 ÷ 2,000, market cap over book value)
1.43x (= 2,000 ÷ 1,400, numerator and denominator reversed)
0.6 billion (= 2,000 − 1,400, taking the difference instead of the ratio)
1.4x (= 1,400 ÷ 1,000, book value rounded down)
quiz.explanation: P/B = Market Cap / Book Value = 1,400/2,000 = 0.7. The market is paying 70 cents for every dong of net assets on the books - either an opportunity, or the market doesn't trust that book figure.

quiz.question: Why is P/B almost useless when valuing a software company?
options: Because software companies aren't allowed to record shareholders' equity
Because value sits in brand and IP, things that aren't on the books
Because a software company's book value is always negative
Because software depreciates so fast the book value is instantly outdated
quiz.explanation: The cost of building a brand and developing products is largely expensed immediately rather than sitting on the balance sheet. Book value therefore misses exactly what creates value, making P/E or EV/EBITDA more suitable.

quiz.question: What is the relationship between P/B and ROE?
options: Multiplying P/B by ROE gives the same company's P/E
P/B and ROE always move in opposite directions
The higher the ROE, the more the market is willing to pay in P/B
The two metrics are independent, with no relationship at all
quiz.explanation: A business generating 20% on each dong of equity is worth more than one generating only 5% on the same capital. This is why high-ROE banks trade above 2x book while low-ROE banks sit below 1x.

keyTakeaways: P/B < 1: cheaper than book - worth investigating why
Most suited to banks, insurance, real estate

practicePrompt.question: A company has Market Cap (market capitalization) = 800 billion, Book Value (book value of shareholders' equity) = 400 billion. What is this company's P/B, and if another company has P/B = 0.7, what does that suggest?
options: P/B = 800/400 = 2x; a P/B below 1 needs investigating, it isn't automatically a bargain
P/B = 400/800 = 0.5, showing the company's debt-to-equity ratio
P/B must always be greater than 1 for every company operating normally; a P/B below 1 signals the company is about to go bankrupt
P/B has nothing to do with book value, it only reflects the profit a company generates
practicePrompt.explanation: P/B = Market Cap / Book Value = 800/400 = 2x. A P/B < 1 (cheaper than book) doesn't automatically mean 'a bargain' - it needs further investigation of asset quality and accompanying ROE, since sometimes the market prices it low for good reason (poorly earning assets, high risk).

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: P/B < 1: cheaper than book - worth investigating why

application.title: Calculate P/B
application.message: Divide Market Cap by Book Value (Equity) for a company, especially try it on a bank or real-estate company - this is where P/B is most meaningful.
application.secondary: If P/B is below 1, don't get excited right away - find the reason before concluding it's an opportunity.

sections.text: P/B (Price-to-Book) compares a stock's market price against its book value (shareholders' equity) per share - a metric especially useful for industries where book-value assets reflect real value fairly closely.

sections.label: The formula
sections.text: P/B = Market Cap / Book Value (Total Equity)
A P/B below 1 isn't automatically an opportunity

During the 2011-2013 Vietnamese bank bad-debt crisis, many bank stocks traded at a P/B below 1. At a glance it looks like 'the stock is cheaper than net asset value' - but in substance the market was worried real asset quality (hidden bad debt not yet fully provisioned for) was much worse than the numbers on the books. This is a classic example of a 'value trap' - looking cheap but actually reflecting real risk accurately.
Why P/B is best suited to banks, insurance, and real estate

P/B is useful when book-value assets reflect real economic value fairly closely: for a bank, that's its loan portfolio; for real estate, it's land and building value. By contrast, for technology companies, book value is usually very low because it doesn't reflect brand value, patents, personnel, or customer data - intangible assets that don't fully appear on a traditional balance sheet.

items: P/B < 1: the market values it below book value - worth investigating why (asset quality, low ROE, industry downturn)
For banks, the quality of book value depends heavily on whether bad-debt provisions are fully made
P/B is best suited to: banks, insurance, real estate - where assets make up most of the business's value
P/B is poorly suited to: technology, services, strong brands - where real value sits in intangible assets

lines: A low P/B is a question that needs answering, not a ready-made answer - always check the quality of the assets behind that book figure.
